newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major rallies troops, slams devolution plans.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major rallies troops, slams devolution plans.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major, dismissing the predictions of opinion polls, told 2,500 flag-waving Conservative supporters on Friday that he intended to retain power in Britain's general election.

"The story of my life is about beating the odds and I intend to beat the odds again on May 1," he told an evening meeting closer in style to a U.S. presidential campaign rally than his standard walkabout style among voters.

Major, whose Conservatives trail the opposition Labour party in the polls by more than 20 points, also seized on what appeared to be a slip by Labour leader Tony Blair over plans for devolving power in Scotland.
He said Labour's policies threatened jobs across Britain, accused the opposition leader of breaking his promises and described his proposals for Scotland as "total and utter chaos."
But Blair, fighting back after his first real setback in the election campaign, charged Major with "triumphalist arrogance."

At a meeting in a small civic hall in central England, chosen to contrast with the slick presentation of Major's rally in London's Albert Hall, Blair said the Conservatives had misread the mood of voters across the country.

"I say to the Tories (Conservatives), you carry on with your glitzy rallies. You carry on bussing in the party faithful," he told several hundred people inside the hall and hundreds more listening on loudspeakers outside.
"Let me go out and have a dialogue with the British people. Let me explain the changes we propose. Let me set out our stall and let the people make their judgement."

Major, who won the 1992 election against the odds but now faces an even bigger opinion poll obstacle, said 18 years of unbroken Conservative rule had produced a prosperity that a Labour government would jeopadrise.
"What is at stake in this election is not just your job. Your livelihood. Your prosperity. It's much more. It's the future of the very land in which we live," he said.
Major rewrote large chunks of his speech to focus on Blair's problems over Scotland, underlining the importance Conservative tacticians give to the row.

Blair gave an interview with the Scotsman newspaper earlier in which he likened any tax powers of a proposed Scottish parliament to those of a parish council and said sovereignty would remain with him as prime minister.

If it wins the May 1 election, Labour intends to hold a referendum in Scotland on setting up a parliament in Edinburgh with the power to vary income tax by as much as three percentage points for Scottish taxpayers.
But after the Scotsman interview Blair came under heavy fire from Scottish journalists who asked what was the point of granting powers if he would not let them be exercised.
Blair defended his comments, saying that the British parliament would constitutionally be devolving powers but not ceding sovereignity if it legislated to create a Scottish parliament.
